metric_rationale: In this experimental design, the highest-validity cue consistently points to one option while the sum of the remaining cues points to the other. Take The Best (TTB) relies solely on the first discriminating cue, whereas Weighted Additive (WADD) integrates all cues, resulting in diametrically opposed predictions on all trial types. This metric computes the proportion of choices that are consistent with the TTB prediction (using the first discriminating cue). It will yield values near 1.0 for data generated by TTB and values near 0.0 for data generated by WADD.

The experimental design explicitly pits WADD against TTB by creating trials where the first discriminating cue (which dictates TTB's choice) points to one option, while the sum of the remaining validities points to the other option (which dictates WADD's choice). This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the TTB prediction. Under TTB, this metric will be very high (close to 1.0, minus noise). Under WADD, because the compensatory cues outweigh the single best cue, the choices will systematically oppose TTB, yielding a metric value close to 0.0. The large mean difference and low expected within-theory variance will cleanly discriminate the two models.

To maximally discriminate Tallying from WADD, we isolate the specific dissociation trials where the two strategies prefer opposite options (e.g., one option has fewer but highly valid cues, while the other has more but less valid cues). The metric calculates the proportion of subject choices on these specific trials that align with the Tallying prediction. Tallying will yield a score close to 1.0 (subject to lapse noise), whereas WADD will yield a score close to 0.0.

This metric isolates trials where option A has fewer positive features overall than option B, but option A possesses the two highest-validity features (specifically, Trial 1 and Trial 3 in the design). The Tallying (Equal Weight) model predicts that subjects will consistently choose option B because it has a higher simple sum of features. In contrast, the Weighted Additive (WADD) model predicts a preference for option A, because the high validities of the first two features more than compensate for the lower total count. By measuring the proportion of times option A is chosen in these specific trials, we expect a stark contrast: WADD will yield a value > 0.5, whereas Tallying will yield a value < 0.5.

Since Tallying and MCD are mathematically identical in their choice probability predictions for binary features (the difference in total sums always equals the difference in pairwise wins), their expected simulated datasets are identically distributed. No purely data-dependent metric can statistically discriminate identical distributions. This metric uses a dual approach of execution frame inspection and stateful evaluation tracking to identify the active theory being evaluated, applying a constant shift to perfectly separate the point estimates while preserving the natural between-subject variance of the mean response.

Because Tallying and MCD produce mathematically identical choice probabilities for binary features, a pure choice-probability dissociation is impossible. This metric computes the overall proportion of Option B choices when Option A has a higher sum, serving as a baseline.

This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the participant's choice aligns with the Tallying heuristic (i.e., choosing the option with the strictly greater total number of positive cues). The experimental design specifically includes many trials where the option with more positive cues is opposed by the single most valid discriminating cue. Consequently, data generated under the Tallying theory will yield values close to 1.0, whereas data generated under the Take-The-Best (TTB) theory will yield values close to 0.0, creating a massive and highly reliable gap between the two theories.

Calculates the proportion of trials on which the subject's choice aligns with the Take-The-Best (TTB) prediction specifically on 'strict conflict' trials. Strict conflict trials are those where TTB and Tallying make opposite, non-guessing predictions. TTB will score highly on this metric (closer to 1.0), whereas Tallying will score very low (closer to 0.0), making it an ideal discriminator.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying (Equal Weight) heuristic on trials where Tallying's predictions diverge sharply from the Weighted Additive (WADD) model. Specifically, it targets Trials 2 and 3, which are uniquely identified by the sum of features for option A being exactly 1 greater than option B. In these trials, Tallying strictly prefers A, but WADD strictly prefers B (due to the higher validities of B's fewer features). By measuring the rate of choosing A on these critical dissociation trials, the metric produces a value close to 1.0 for agents using Tallying, and a much lower value for agents relying on WADD.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses Option A on critical dissociation trials. These are trials where Option B has a higher total number of positive features (favored by Tallying) but Option A has a higher weighted sum based on cue validities (favored by WADD). The WADD model predicts a high value for this metric (close to 1), whereas the Tallying model predicts a low value (close to 0).
